# The Declare homepage

The page you are reading, written in Declare. The design tokens live once as
semantic type components, and the page is a vertical **flow** of auto-sizing
sections — no absolute-y. Each section's height falls out of its content, so
the page stacks and re-flows on its own at any width. The full-bleed chrome —
the blueprint grid, the sticky header, the pointer dot — sits absolutely
around the centered column.

`{ }` bodies are TypeScript, so colors there are `0x…`; `[ ]` literal slots
take `#…`. Every color on the page has a name in the App's `theme` record —
the palette lives there, once, and nowhere else.

segments.html:
font Sans [ family = "system-ui" ]

font Mono [ family = "ui-monospace" ]

segments.md:
## The figures under an app card

`stats.json` is generated by the prewarm pass from the real production builds
(line metrics + the gzipped wire size), so these helpers are the only place the
page decides how to *say* a figure — never what it is. A missing value yields
"", so a card that outruns the stats file degrades to no figures rather than to
"undefined".

Each figure arrives as its OWN argument, because a helper's arguments are its
reactive wiring. Hand it the whole record instead and the reads happen inside
the body, where the dependency extractor cannot see them — the compiler refuses
that (DECLARE7001), and it is right to: the line would render once against an
unloaded DataSource and never update again.

segments.html:
script {
    function hpLines(total: object, code: object, comment: object): string {
        if (total == null) return ""
        return total + " lines — " + code + " code, " + comment + " comment"
        }

    function hpWire(wire: object): string {
        return wire == null ? "" : " · " + Math.round((wire as any) / 1024) + " KB over the wire"
        }
    }

## Type as tokens

Every text style on the page is one of these classes — headings semibold with
tracking that scales with the size, eyebrows mono and wide-tracked, lead and
body in the muted tone — so the page's whole typography reskins from here.

segments.html:
class Heading extends Text [ fontWeight = semibold, textColor = { theme.text },
    letterSpacing = { -0.02 * fontSize }, selectable = true
    ]


class Eyebrow extends Text [ fontFamily = [Mono, "monospace"], fontSize = 13,
    fontWeight = semibold, letterSpacing = 1.6, textColor = { theme.muted }, selectable = true
    ]


// the accent section number

class Marker extends Eyebrow [ textColor = { theme.accent } ]

// footer text in the Declare typeface (App Sans), not the mono eyebrow

class FootLabel extends Text [ fontSize = 13, fontWeight = semibold, textColor = { theme.muted }, selectable = true ]

class Lead extends Text [ fontSize = 19, fontWeight = normal, textColor = { theme.lead }, selectable = true ]

class Body extends Text [ fontSize = 17, fontWeight = normal, textColor = { theme.muted }, selectable = true ]

// an article paragraph (the "Why" view) — HTML flow, so its `"""` source wraps
// at the writer’s margin and the line breaks collapse away in the rendering

class Para extends HTMLText [ fontSize = 18, lineHeight = 1.2, width = { parent.width },
    bodyColor = { theme.lead }, selectable = true
    ]

segments.md:
## The header pills

A nav link is a padded pill: it fills with surface-2 on hover (a rounded rect
behind the text, not just a color change), and `pressed` deepens the pill and
lights the label — the tap feedback a touch device gets in place of hover.
Width auto-fits the label plus 12px of padding each side.

segments.html:
class NavLink extends View [ height = 33, cornerRadius = 8,
    label:   string = "",
    url:     string = "",
    to:      string = "",
    at:      string = "",

    // pressed deepens the pill + lights the label — the tap feedback a touch
    // device gets in place of hover (mouseDown/Up fire on a tap, hover does not).

    fill = { pressed ? theme.pillPress : hovered ? theme.pillHover : null },

    // A pill goes one of three ways: `to` is an in-app location (a fragment —
    // write `app.location`); `at` names a SECTION of that location's flow, and
    // lands on it instead of the top; `url` is an out-of-app target (the
    // `navigate` service action, capabilities.md §6). Never more than one door.

    onClick()     { if (classroot.to != "") { app.location = classroot.to; if (classroot.at != "") app.toSection(classroot.at); else app.toTop() } else if (classroot.url != "") app.navigate(classroot.url) },
    lbl: Text [ x = 12, y = 8, fontFamily = [Sans, "system-ui", "sans-serif"], fontSize = 14,
        text = { classroot.label },
        textColor = { classroot.hovered || classroot.pressed ? theme.text : theme.muted } ],
    width = { this.lbl.width + 24 }
    ]

segments.md:
## The mobile nav sheet

At phone width the pill row would ride the wordmark, so it collapses to a kebab
(the page's dot motif) that opens this sheet: a thumb-height row per destination,
drawn from the same `navItems` as the pills. Same press feedback as a pill.

The sheet is the one surface that can afford STRUCTURE. The pill row is bounded
by the window's width, so a destination with children shows there as a single
pill; the sheet is already open by the time it is read and vertical space is
free, so the children get their own rows under the parent — no second tap to
reach the thing you came for. One `navItems` list, two renditions, which is
what these two surfaces already were.

segments.html:
class MobileNavRow extends View [ width = { parent.width }, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8,
    label:   string = "",
    url:     string = "",
    to:      string = "",
    at:      string = "",

    // a child row: same type size and the same thumb height as its parent —
    // these are destinations, not annotations, and shrinking them would say
    // otherwise. The INDENT alone carries the hierarchy, with the quieter
    // tone behind it.

    sub:     boolean = false,

    fill = { pressed ? theme.pillPress : hovered ? theme.pillHover : null },
    onClick()     { app.menuOpen = false; if (classroot.to != "") { app.location = classroot.to; if (classroot.at != "") app.toSection(classroot.at); else app.toTop() } else if (classroot.url != "") app.navigate(classroot.url) },

    lbl: Text [ x = { classroot.sub ? 30 : 14 }, y = center, fontFamily = [Sans, "system-ui", "sans-serif"],
        fontSize = 16, fontWeight = medium,
        text = { classroot.label },
        textColor = { classroot.hovered || classroot.pressed ? theme.text : classroot.sub ? theme.muted : theme.lead } ]
    ]


// one navItems entry as it appears in the sheet: its own row, then a row per
// child. `:children[]` on an entry whose list is empty resolves to no records,
// so a childless destination is simply its own row — there is no branch here
// and no second rendition to keep in step.

class MobileNavGroup extends View [ width = { parent.width },
    height = { this.contentHeight },
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 0 ],
    MobileNavRow [ label = { :label }, to = { :to }, at = { :at }, url = { :url } ],
    kids: View [ width = { parent.width }, height = { this.contentHeight },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 0 ],
        MobileNavRow [ datapath = :children[], sub = true,
            label = { :label }, to = { :to }, at = { :at }, url = { :url } ]
        ]
    ]

segments.md:
## Section furniture

The repeated shapes the numbered sections are built from: an `AppCard` (§01 —
a shot of a real application over its one-line description), a `FeatureRow`
for the closing enumeration, a `Point` with its accent top-rule, a big
gradient `Metric`, and the footer’s separator `Dot`.

### A screenshot frame

A clipped, rounded plate holding one app’s picture. Its height derives from its
OWN width at the shots’ 1.6 aspect, so whatever sizes it — a responsive share,
a layout, a card — gets the right box with no second number to keep in sync.
Clicking runs the app; the stroke lifts to the accent rule on hover so the
plate reads as a door rather than a picture.

segments.html:
class Shot extends View [
    src: string = "",
    url: string = "",

    // An optional MOVING version. `clip` is taken — it is View's own attribute —
    // so the moving source is `motion`, and the still becomes its poster:
    // `pic` shows until the clip has a frame, which is the composition a
    // `poster` attribute would have hard-coded. `live` gates playback, so a
    // clip below the fold is not decoding while nobody is looking.

    motion: string = "",
    live: boolean = true,

    // an outside hover — the card's own title — lights the plate too, so the
    // picture and the words behave as the single target they are

    hot: boolean = false,

    cornerRadius = 12, clip = true, fill = { theme.stage },
    height = { this.width / 1.6 },

    // A GLOW, not a drop shadow. On a near-black ground a black shadow has
    // nothing to darken — it reads as almost nothing. A light halo does the
    // same job in the other direction: zero offset so it sits evenly around the
    // plate, and a low alpha so it separates the shot from the page without
    // announcing itself. The 1px stroke is still the crisp edge; this is the
    // separation behind it.

    stroke = { stroke(1, hovered || hot ? theme.pointRule : theme.line) },

    // colours here are RRGGBBAA (the theme's own spelling — `scrim` is
    // 0x0B141BB3), so the alpha is the LOW byte: a cool off-white at 0x1C
    // resting, 0x33 when the card is hot.

    shadow = { shadow(0, 0, 26, hovered || hot ? 0xBFD8EA8C : 0xBFD8EA4D) },

    onClick() { if (classroot.url != "") app.navigate(classroot.url) },

    pic: Image [ width = { parent.width }, height = { parent.height },
        stretches = both, source = { classroot.src },
        visible = { classroot.motion == "" || !this.parent.reel.loaded } ],

    reel: Video [ visible = { classroot.motion != "" },
        width = { parent.width }, height = { parent.height }, stretches = both,
        loop = true, source = { classroot.motion },
        playing = { classroot.live && classroot.motion != "" } ]
    ]

The page’s quiet link rendition — the accent, brightening on hover and flashing

selectable: it is a control, not copy.

### A compact figure

`Metric`’s narrow-column sibling. Metric sizes for a full-width band and goes
full-width below 560, which is right there and wrong inside a half-column: three
of them would stack into a tower. This one stays three-up in the space it is
given.

segments.html:
class MiniMetric extends View [
    value: string = "",
    note:  string = "",
    width = { (parent.width - 40) / 3 },
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 4 ],
    Heading [ fontSize = 34, width = { parent.width }, textFill = { theme.brand },
        text = { classroot.value } ],
    Body [ fontSize = 12, width = { parent.width }, text = { classroot.note } ]
    ]

segments.md:
### An application card

The tracker and the desktop: a screenshot over the app’s name, what it does as
one dot-separated run, its figures small and dim, and a source link. The plate
and the name run the app; the source link opens the reader — and because events
do not bubble, that link answers its own click without the card also firing.

segments.html:
class AppCard extends View [
    title:   string = "",
    shot:    string = "",
    blurb:   string = "",
    figures: string = "",
    url:     string = "",
    srcUrl:  string = "",
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 16 ],

    // TWO hover facts, not one. `titleHot` is the words; `hot` is the words or
    // the plate. The plate reads `titleHot` and the words read `hot`, so a
    // pointer anywhere on either lights BOTH — and there is no cycle, because
    // each derives from the raw `hovered` of the other, never from its styling.

    titleHot: boolean = { this.head.name.hovered || this.head.arrow.hovered },
    hot: boolean = { this.frame.hovered || this.titleHot },

    // the name LEADS: you read what the thing is, then look at it. The plate
    // under a title also gives the row a left edge to hang from, which three
    // pictures of different interiors do not.

    head: View [ width = { parent.width }, height = { this.contentHeight },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 10 ],
        name: Heading [ fontSize = 22, wrap = false, selectable = false,
            textColor = { classroot.hot ? theme.accent : theme.text },
            text = { classroot.title },
            onClick() { app.navigate(classroot.url) }
            ],
        arrow: Text [ y = 3, fontSize = 16, fontWeight = semibold, wrap = false,
            textColor = { classroot.hot ? theme.accent : theme.dim }, text = "→",
            onClick() { app.navigate(classroot.url) }
            ]
        ],

    frame: Shot [ width = { parent.width }, src = { classroot.shot }, url = { classroot.url },
        hot = { classroot.titleHot } ],

    copy: View [ width = { parent.width },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],
        say: Body [ fontSize = 15, width = { parent.width }, text = { classroot.blurb } ],
        fig: Body [ fontSize = 13, width = { parent.width }, textColor = { theme.dim },
            text = { classroot.figures } ],
        src: SmallLink [ text = "View & edit source →", url = { classroot.srcUrl } ]
        ]
    ]

segments.md:
### A feature row

One block of the closing enumeration: the category, then its points beneath.
Two levels of replication and no list-building code — the block comes from a
slice of `:rows[]`, each point from `:items[]` inside it, so the section's
shape is written once and the data decides how many there are.

The points are PHRASES, not sentences: a run of prose here reads as a
document, and this has to read as a layout. The blocks pair into two columns
at the section level (below), which is also what keeps a label from stranding
across a wide gutter from the points it names.

segments.html:
class FeatureRow extends View [ width = { parent.width },
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],

    cap: Heading [ fontSize = 15, width = { parent.width }, selectable = true,
        text = { "" + :cap } ],

    list: View [ width = { parent.width },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 7 ],
        Body [ datapath = :items[], fontSize = 15, width = { parent.width },
            text = { "" + this.$data("") } ]
        ]
    ]


class Point extends View [ width = { Math.min(357, parent.width) },
    ptitle: string = "",
    body:   string = "",
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 16 ],
    rule: View [ width = { parent.width }, height = 2, fill = { theme.pointRule } ],
    txt: View [ width = { parent.width },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
        Heading [ fontSize = 17, text = { classroot.ptitle } ],
        Body    [ fontSize = 15, width = { parent.width }, text = { classroot.body } ]
        ]
    ]


// width/fontSize key off parent.width (the real available width in the row) —
// a component sizes off its parent, not the app; `app.width` is the whole page

class Metric extends View [
    cols: number = 2,
    width = { parent.width < 560 ? parent.width : (parent.width - 48 * (cols - 1)) / cols },
    value: string = "",
    note:  string = "",
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    Heading [ fontSize = { parent.width < 420 ? 54 : 92 }, width = { parent.width }, textAlign = center,
        textFill = { theme.brand }, text = { classroot.value } ],
    Body [ fontSize = 14, width = { parent.width }, textAlign = center, text = { classroot.note } ]
    ]


class Dot extends Body [ fontSize = 14, textColor = { theme.faint }, text = "·" ]

segments.md:
## Buttons

Primary fills accent and brightens on hover; secondary lifts to surface-2 and
answers a press with an accent ring. Press feedback is what a touch device
sees in place of hover — both are driven by the view’s own handlers.

segments.html:
class Button extends View [ height = 46, cornerRadius = 9,
    label:   string = "",
    primary: boolean = true,
    fill = { primary ? (pressed ? theme.accentPress : hovered ? theme.accentHover : theme.accent)
                     : (pressed ? theme.press       : hovered ? theme.hover       : theme.surface) },
    stroke = { primary ? stroke(0, theme.accent) : stroke(1, pressed ? theme.accent2 : theme.line) },

    // label centered in the button box (textAlign over the full width)

    caption: Text [ y = 14, width = { parent.width }, textAlign = center, fontSize = 15, fontWeight = semibold,
        text = { classroot.label },
        textColor = { classroot.primary ? theme.ink : theme.text } ]
    ]

segments.md:
## The site footer

One line, shared by every page of the site — the scrolling front page and the
in-app Why / Language views alike: provenance left, legal right.

A `FootLink` is the footer’s link rendition: the eyebrow treatment with the
teal hover and the brighter pressed tap feedback, navigating on click.

segments.html:
class FootLink extends FootLabel [
    to: string = "",

    // A navigating link is a control, not copy — FootLabel's `selectable`
    // is for the static footer text and must not ride along here.

    selectable = false,
    textColor = { pressed ? theme.accent2Press : hovered ? theme.accent2 : theme.muted },
    onClick()     { app.navigate(to) }
    ]


// the footer separator: a faint dot that drops out once the row wraps, so no dot
// is ever stranded at a line's end (the 620 line is where the row stops fitting)

class FootSep extends FootLabel [ text = "·", textColor = { theme.faint }, visible = { parent.width >= 620 } ]

class Footer extends View [ width = { parent.width },
    // its own bottom margin — the page has no trailing spacer, because the
    // flow's section spacing applied to that too and left a large dead band

    height = { this.contentHeight + 36 },
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 16 ],

    // one centered flow — every item on a line, dot-separated at full width. As
    // the width narrows the separator dots drop out and the items wrap to centered
    // rows (the wider spacing keeps them legible), so provenance and legal never
    // collide the way a left/right split does. Dropping the dots on wrap is what
    // avoids a stranded separator at a line's end.

    row: View [ width = { parent.width }, height = { this.contentHeight },
        layout: WrappingLayout [ align = center, spacing = { parent.width >= 620 ? 10 : 18 }, lineSpacing = 10 ],

        // "Built in Declare" is one text RUN (HTMLText carries the brand accent
        // inline), so it keeps a word space, not a gap

        built: HTMLText [ width = 108, fontSize = 13, fontWeight = semibold, bodyColor = { theme.muted },
            accents = { ({ g: theme.brand }) },
            html = "Built in <span class='g'>Declare</span>" ],
        FootSep [ ],
        FootLink [ to = "apps/homepage/homepage.declare?viewer", text = "View Source" ],
        FootSep [ ],
        FootLink [ to = "apps/docs/docs.declare", text = "Docs" ],
        FootSep [ ],
        FootLink [ to = "https://github.com/davidtemkin/declarelang", text = "GitHub" ],
        FootSep [ ],
        lic: FootLink [ to = "https://github.com/davidtemkin/declarelang/blob/main/LICENSE", text = "MIT License" ],
        FootSep [ ],
        FootLabel [ text = "© 2026 David Temkin" ]
        ]
    ]

segments.md:
## The live panels

The heart of the page: every demo is real Declare, compiled and running. A
`CodeField` is a native editable field seeded (uncontrolled, `initial`) from
the demo’s source — it follows the source until you type, then holds the
edit, publishing each keystroke on `App.liveSource` for the host to
recompile. A `SourcePanel` frames it (LIVE·EDITABLE chip, Revert, hairline);
a `PreviewFrame` hosts the compiled app as an **embedded child app** — no
iframe — so the preview can’t drift from the source. Its `active` flag gates
the island slot, which is what bounds the full-page-editor recursion: a
closed editor’s preview renders nothing, so the page source containing that
very editor only descends one level per user click.

segments.html:
class CodeField extends TextInput [ multiline = true, spellcheck = false,
    fontFamily = [Mono, "monospace"], fontSize = 11, textColor = { theme.lead },
    editName: string = "",
    src: string = "",
    initial = { src },
    onInput() { app.liveCard = editName; app.liveSource = text }
    ]


// `height` is set per demo (at the use site) to sit just above what the code /
// preview needs; Revert restores the pristine `src` and asks the host to recompile

class SourcePanel extends View [
    editName: string = "",
    src: string = "",
    fill = { theme.panel }, cornerRadius = 12, stroke = { stroke(1, theme.panelLine) },

    // the affordance chip: this code runs, and you can type in it

    live: View [ x = 12, y = 7, height = 18, cornerRadius = 5, fill = { theme.accent },
        width = { this.t.width + 14 },
        t: Text [ x = 7, y = 4, fontFamily = [Sans, "system-ui"], fontSize = 9, fontWeight = bold,
            letterSpacing = 0.8, wrap = false, textColor = { theme.ink }, text = "LIVE · EDITABLE" ]
        ],
    revert: View [ y = 5, height = 20, cornerRadius = 6, stroke = { stroke(1, theme.revertLine) },
        x = { parent.width - this.width - 10 },
        width = { this.rlbl.width + 16 },
        fill = { hovered ? theme.hover : null },
        onClick() { classroot.field.text = classroot.src
                    app.liveCard = classroot.editName
                    app.liveSource = classroot.src },
        rlbl: Text [ x = 8, y = 3, fontFamily = [Sans, "system-ui"], fontSize = 11, fontWeight = semibold,
            textColor = { parent.hovered ? theme.text : theme.lead }, text = "Revert" ]
        ],
    hairline: View [ y = 31, width = { parent.width }, height = 1, fill = { theme.panelLine } ],
    field: CodeField [ x = 12, y = 40, width = { parent.width - 24 }, height = { parent.height - 48 },
        editName = { classroot.editName }, src = { classroot.src } ],

    // the compile report, at the panel — a broken edit shows its error right here
    // (the last good preview keeps running beside it); host feeds app.liveReport

    err: View [ width = { parent.width }, fill = { theme.errBg },
        visible = { app.liveCard == classroot.editName && app.liveReport != "" },
        y = { parent.height - this.height },
        height = { this.msg.height + 16 },
        bar: View [ x = 0, y = 0, width = 3, height = { parent.height }, fill = { theme.errBar } ],
        msg: Text [ x = 14, y = 8, width = { parent.width - 28 }, wrap = true,
            fontFamily = [Mono, "monospace"], fontSize = 11, textColor = { theme.errText },
            text = { app.liveReport } ]
        ]
    ]


class PreviewFrame extends View [
    runName: string = "",
    active: boolean = true,
    run: AppIsland [ width = { parent.width }, height = { parent.height },
        program = { classroot.active ? classroot.runName : "" } ]
    ]

segments.md:
## Backdrop and section heads

The blueprint grid draws itself; a `SectionHead` is the tight
number · heading · lead rhythm every numbered section opens with.

The blueprint backdrop is VIEWPORT-sized and pinned, never document-sized.

`draw()` rasterises into a canvas the size of the view's bounds at device pixel
ratio, so a backdrop stretched over a whole document allocates a backing store
for the whole document: the language view is 16,711px tall, which at 2x is a
2882 x 33,422 canvas — 96 megapixels, ~385 MB, reallocated every time the view
is shown or hidden. Measured: 1091 ms blocked going in, 1435 ms coming back.
Viewport-sized and pinned: 57 ms and 21 ms. (It also cleared Chrome's 32,767px
maximum canvas dimension, which the old shape exceeded.)

A uniform 32px lattice looks the same pinned as it does scrolling, so this
costs nothing visually — it is the same paper, drawn once.

segments.html:
class GridBg extends View [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.fillStyle = theme.grid
        for (let gx = 0; gx <= width;  gx += 32) d.fillRect(gx, 0, 1, height)
        for (let gy = 0; gy <= height; gy += 32) d.fillRect(0, gy, width, 1)
        }
    ]


class SectionHead extends View [ width = { parent.width },
    num:  string = "",
    head: string = "",
    lead: string = "",
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 14 ],
    Marker  [ text = { classroot.num } ],
    Heading [ fontSize = 40, width = { Math.min(900, parent.width) }, text = { classroot.head } ],
    Lead    [ width = { Math.min(760, parent.width) }, text = { classroot.lead } ]
    ]

segments.md:
## The page

The palette lives once as a prevailing `theme` token record — every semantic
type class defaults its color to `{ theme.… }`, so the whole page reskins
from this one place. The scroller fills the viewport and scrolls its taller
content natively; the chrome further down (header, cursor) are its
**siblings**, not its children, so they never move.

segments.html:
// THE HEADLINE LIVES HERE, ONCE. The hero reads it, and `appName` carries it
// into `document.title` at boot (runtime/src/boot.ts — "the ONE place that
// mapping lives"), which is also what the crawl extraction reports as the
// page's title and what the bake stamps into index.html's <title> and social
// cards. Before this, index.html restated the headline by hand in six places;
// changing the hero left all six behind, and the drift was invisible to a
// visitor — the runtime overwrites document.title at boot — so only crawlers
// and LLMs ever read the stale copy. Exactly the readers this page is for.

App [ tagline: string = "a UI language for you and your AI",
    appName = { "Declare — " + app.tagline },
    theme = { {
        // text, brightest to faintest
        text: 0xE7EEF2, lead: 0x9DB0BC, muted: 0x8A9BA6, dim: 0x6A7C89, faint: 0x556673,
        // the blue accent and its interaction shades; links brighten past accent
        // (hover), then flash brighter still at the press — the same direction
        // FootLink's teal takes, so every text link answers a tap the same way
        accent: 0x4C8DFF, accentHover: 0x63A0FF, accentPress: 0x3D7BE0, linkHover: 0x7FB0FF, linkPress: 0xB2CFFF,
        // the teal second accent; the brand gradient runs accent → accent2
        accent2: 0x37E0C8, accent2Press: 0x9BF2E4,
        brand: gradient("90deg", 0x4C8DFF, 0x37E0C8),

A leading `#` is this app's own location — the fragment IS `app.location`

nothing else wired. Anything else leaves through the `navigate` service

§6) and they are the right tool for landing inside a long page — but the
reveal resolves in the same frame as the location write, while rendered

the DOM backend's ResizeObserver), so an anchor into this essay lands
against a half-built page. Measured: the target's y read 711 on the

            // 32px and left dead space under the footer (measured: 5243 →
            // 5412 over six trips). Reading the content's extent is what the
            // document-tall version did too, and it is not a cycle: the
            // content never reads the backdrop.

            y = { Math.max(0, Math.min(Math.floor(app.scrollY / 32) * 32,
                    parent.body.y + parent.body.height - this.height)) },

        body: View [ y = 56, width = { app.width }, selectable = true,
            col: View [ width = { Math.min(720, app.width - 48) }, x = { Math.max(24, (app.width - 720) / 2) }, y = 52,
                layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 22 ],
                Marker  [ text = "WHY DECLARE" ],
                Heading [ fontSize = { app.width < 700 ? 32 : 42 }, width = { parent.width },
                    text = "Why a new language, now?" ],
                Para [ html = """
                    Start with the obvious objection. LLMs write code now, and they’re
                    best at the languages they’ve seen the most — so the winning move is
                    to use whatever has the biggest corpus and let the model figure it
                    out. By that logic the era of new programming languages is over.
                    """ ],
                Para [ html = """
                    That argument gets its facts right and its conclusion backwards.
                    Producing code is now nearly free; trusting it costs what it always
                    did. An LLM writing React verifies its work by resemblance — this
                    looks like the billion lines it trained on — and resemblance is not
                    correctness. Meanwhile, less and less of the code passes under human
                    eyes, which leaves the language and its compiler as the one reviewer
                    that is always present. Handing the writing to a machine doesn’t make
                    the language irrelevant. It makes it load-bearing.
                    """ ],
                Heading [ fontSize = 24, width = { parent.width }, text = "Two kinds of leverage" ],
                Para [ html = """
                    What an LLM gets from a mainstream stack is corpus leverage: fluency
                    by imitation — broad, shallow, self-contradictory, unverifiable. The
                    other kind is comprehension leverage: a language small enough to hand
                    to a model whole, regular enough that its programs can be analyzed
                    rather than pattern-matched, and backed by a compiler that turns each
                    mistake into a precise correction. Corpus leverage arrives free with
                    popularity. Comprehension leverage has to be designed in — and it is
                    the only kind a new language can compete on.
                    """ ],
                Para [ html = """
                    This is a measured bet, not a hunch. LLMs can learn a language they
                    never trained on from a spec in context — in recent studies, a small
                    language purpose-designed for LLM use, with zero training exposure,
                    beat the same model writing Python, its best-trained language. And
                    what bounds a model’s ability to repair its own mistakes is the
                    quality of the feedback: a compiler that explains beats one that
                    merely rejects, by a double-digit margin.
                    """ ],

                    layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [({ from: 560, flow: "row", gap: 20 }), ({ from: 0, flow: "stack", gap: 8 })] } ],
                    lbl: Text [ fontSize = 14, wrap = false, textColor = { theme.faint }, text = "The studies:" ],
                    s1: Text [ fontSize = 14, wrap = false, selectable = false,
                        textColor = { this.pressed ? theme.linkPress : this.hovered ? theme.linkHover : theme.accent }, text = "a zero-corpus DSL vs. Python →",
                        onClick()     { app.navigate("https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23214") }
                        ],
                    s2: Text [ fontSize = 14, wrap = false, selectable = false,
                        textColor = { this.pressed ? theme.linkPress : this.hovered ? theme.linkHover : theme.accent }, text = "feedback quality vs. repair →",
                        onClick()     { app.navigate("https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06939") }
                        ]
                    ],
                Heading [ fontSize = 24, width = { parent.width }, text = "Designed in, not bolted on" ],
                Para [ html = """
                    Declare’s declarative layer is small — the whole language fits in a
                    model’s context window with room left for your app — and everything
                    inside a { } is ordinary TypeScript, so the hard part of generation
                    rides the largest corpus there is. Where Declare looks familiar, it
                    behaves the way a model — or you — will assume: assignment is
                    assignment, and there is no bypass to forget. Where it’s genuinely
                    new, it looks new — brackets for structure, :path for data — a
                    visible cue to consult the spec instead of autocompleting from memory.
                    """ ],
                Para [ html = """
                    And because a UI’s real structure — components, state, data, what
                    reacts to what — is expressed in the language, the compiler can see
                    all of it: it extracts every binding’s dependencies statically,
                    checks the shape of the tree, and types the seams. What a model
                    reasons about is exactly what the compiler verifies, and its errors
                    are written for that loop — each one states the rule and names the
                    rewrite that fixes it, because the primary reader of a compiler
                    message, now, is an LLM deciding what to do next.
                    """ ],
                Para [ html = """
                    Indexable content is there from the start: the compiler runs your
                    program at build time and serializes what it renders, so what a
                    visitor sees and what a crawler sees can never drift. No server-side
                    rendering, no hydration. That’s why this page works on a static host
                    like GitHub Pages.
                    """ ],
                Heading [ fontSize = 24, width = { parent.width }, text = "What it’s actually for" ],
                Para [ html = """
                    All of that is the floor, not the point. The point is what a language
                    makes sayable. The most prized layer of modern UI — the continuity
                    you feel in the best native software, where a view doesn’t switch so
                    much as become the next one, where motion carries meaning and
                    everything stays interruptible — has always been bespoke: specialist
                    craft, one interaction at a time, locked to a platform. It is also
                    the least machine-writable code there is; the corpus is thin, custom,
                    and wrong in ways nothing catches.
                    """ ],
                Para [ html = """
                    Declare makes continuity the grain, not the garnish. Motion is a
                    Spring on an attribute; layout is a reactive slot; a mode is a
                    reversible state — so the continuous version of an interface is often
                    less code than the discrete one. The reference app is a calendar
                    whose four views are one surface seen through a moving, zooming
                    rectangle — normally a bespoke project of its own, here a few hundred
                    lines of declarations, readable end to end, written with an LLM. The
                    whole category moves into the declarative, analyzable layer: the
                    hardest part of ambitious UX becomes the part a model is best at.
                    """ ],
                Para [ html = """
                    And that is the forward-looking wager. There is another generation of
                    experiences beyond the hand-crafted best-in-class interfaces of
                    today — built on a foundation with continuity at its core, enabled
                    at the language level, deployed as universally as a URL, and iterated
                    by imaginative designer-developers working with an LLM at their side.
                    Declare is built to find that out.
                    """ ],
                Para [ html = """
                    None of this trades away the human. What makes code legible to a
                    model is what makes it fast for you to read — and you are still the
                    reader who decides. You don’t teach an LLM Declare with a million
                    examples. You hand it the language and let the compiler keep it
                    honest. The corpus will come; the language doesn’t need it first.
                    """ ],

    header: View [ ignoreScroll = true, width = { app.width }, height = 56, y = 0, opacity = 1, fill = { theme.surface },
        hairline: View [ y = 55, width = { app.width }, height = 1, fill = { theme.line } ],

segments.md:
The header row, gutter to gutter. ONE ResponsiveLayout decides whether
the pill row fits, and `share: 0` IS the hiding — so there is no width
test written by hand and no `visible` to keep in step with a number.
Above the threshold the plan drops the kebab; below it the plan drops
the pills and the kebab takes over, the whole list moving to the sheet.
Nothing is ever dropped from the list itself, unlike a progressively
trimmed pill row.

The threshold is the row's OWN width, not the window's (a plan watches
its view), and it is measured: the wordmark runs 53 and the pills 477,
so 593 leaves 63 between them. It is also the one number that moves
when `navItems` gains an entry — which is why it is stated once.
(Was 772 against a 656px pill run, when the three applications each
had a pill of their own; folding them under `Apps` took 179 out of
the row, so the pills now survive to a much narrower window.)

The Spacer is what right-aligns the run: it absorbs the slack between
the wordmark and whatever follows. Shares fill; naturals align.

segments.html:
bar: View [ x = { app.gutter }, y = 0, height = 56,
            width = { app.width - app.gutter * 2 },
            layout: ResponsiveLayout [ gap = 0, plan = { [
                ({ from: 593, flow: "row", share: ({ kebab: 0 }) }),
                ({ from: 0,   flow: "row", share: ({ nav: 0 }) })] } ],

            // wordmark — the product name in the brand gradient, in the hero's typeface

            brand: View [ y = 18, height = 22,
                layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 0 ],
                onClick() { app.location = "home"; app.toTop() },
                Heading [ fontSize = 15, textFill = { theme.brand }, text = "Declare" ]
                ],

            Spacer [ ],

            // primary nav — one NavLink per navItems entry; the padded pills carry
            // their own spacing

            nav: View [ y = 11,
                layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 2 ],
                datapath = { app.navSource.value },
                NavLink [ datapath = :items[], label = { :label }, to = { :to }, at = { :at }, url = { :url } ]
                ],

            // the kebab — three stacked dots (the page's dot motif), the pill's own
            // press feedback, toggling the sheet

            kebab: View [ y = 11, width = 34, height = 33, cornerRadius = 8,
                fill = { pressed ? theme.pillPress : hovered ? theme.pillHover : null },
                onClick()     { app.menuOpen = !app.menuOpen },
                d1: View [ x = center, y = 8,  width = 3, height = 3, cornerRadius = 1.5, fill = { parent.hovered || parent.pressed ? theme.text : theme.muted } ],
                d2: View [ x = center, y = 15, width = 3, height = 3, cornerRadius = 1.5, fill = { parent.hovered || parent.pressed ? theme.text : theme.muted } ],
                d3: View [ x = center, y = 22, width = 3, height = 3, cornerRadius = 1.5, fill = { parent.hovered || parent.pressed ? theme.text : theme.muted } ]
                ]
            ]
        ],

    // pointer dot — a 10px accent-2 dot in VIEWPORT space that SPRINGS after the
    // pointer (loose + low-mass = the slower, longer trail). Two position
    // Springs; the native cursor stays visible and leads, the dot follows.

    pointerDot: View [ ignoreScroll = true, width = 10, height = 10, cornerRadius = 5, fill = { theme.accent2 }, opacity = 0.9,
        shadow = { shadow(0, 0, 12, theme.accent2) },

        // Decoration, not a target: the dot settles exactly under a resting
        // cursor, and the hit chain is occlusion-correct — without this line
        // the dot swallows every hover and press the moment the mouse stops
        // (links lit only while the cursor was moving; clicks resolved, but
        // `pressed`/`hovered` styling died at rest).

        pointerEvents = "none",

        // Only for a HOVERING pointer (mouse / trackpad) — `app.hovering` is false
        // for touch, so the dot never appears on a phone, yet an iPad trackpad
        // (which reports a "mouse" pointer) still gets it. Also yields to the
        // native I-beam when the pointer is over an editable field.

        visible = { app.hovering && !app.pointerOverText },
        followX: Spring [ attribute = x, to = { app.pointerX - 5 },
            stiffness = 120, damping = 14, mass = 0.6, epsilon = 0.05 ],
        followY: Spring [ attribute = y, to = { app.pointerY - 5 },
            stiffness = 120, damping = 14, mass = 0.6, epsilon = 0.05 ]
        ],

    // the mobile nav sheet — the kebab's menu, above everything. A dim scrim below
    // the header catches an outside tap (and leaves the header + kebab lit, so the
    // kebab still toggles it shut); the top-right panel lists every destination as
    // a thumb-height row, replicated from the SAME navData as the pills. Auto-hides
    // if the window is widened back past the breakpoint.

    navSheet: View [ ignoreScroll = true, visible = { app.menuOpen && app.header.bar.kebab.visible }, width = { app.width }, height = { app.height },
        scrim: View [ y = 56, width = { parent.width }, height = { parent.height - 56 }, fill = { theme.scrim },
            onClick() { app.menuOpen = false }
            ],
        panel: View [ x = { app.width - app.gutter - this.width }, y = 62, width = 236, cornerRadius = 12,
            fill = { theme.surface }, shadow = { shadow(0, 12, 40, theme.shade) },

            // DERIVED from the list, not counted: rows and group children are
            // no longer one uniform height, so `navItems.length * 44` stated a
            // relationship the sheet had already stopped having.

            height = { this.list.contentHeight + 12 },
            list: View [ x = 6, y = 6, width = { parent.width - 12 }, height = { this.contentHeight },
                layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 0 ],
                datapath = { app.navSource.value },
                MobileNavGroup [ datapath = :items[] ]
                ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
